notes: Five things a formatter has to know. FIRST, THE MONTH NAMES ARE RUSSIAN-DERIVED, not Turkish: yanvar, fevral, mart, aprel, not Ocak, Subat, Mart, Nisan. They arrived in the Soviet period and were not replaced after 1991. Note sentabr and oktabr WITHOUT the y that Russian and Azerbaijani write, while noyabr keeps it. SECOND, THE DAY TAKES A HYPHEN BEFORE THE MONTH. Uzbek writes 5-mart, not 5 mart, because the day number is an ordinal and the hyphen is how Uzbek attaches an ordinal suffix to a numeral. LL is therefore D-MMMM YYYY. THE FULLY IDIOMATIC FORM GOES FURTHER and cannot be expressed with these tokens alone: an Uzbek document writes 2026-yil 5-mart, year first with the literal word yil attached to it by a hyphen. If the implementation supports literal text in a pattern, LL should become YYYY-[yil] D-MMMM; if it does not, D-MMMM YYYY is the correct fallback and is what is set above. THIRD, monthsInDate is IDENTICAL to months, which is correct and not a copy-paste slip: Uzbek has no genitive or partitive month form, and the case suffix in a date attaches to the day numeral, not to the month. FOURTH, the weekday names are Persian and numbered — dushanba is day two, seshanba day three, chorshanba day four, payshanba day five — with juma (Arabic, Friday prayer) and shanba breaking the count. The array is Sunday-first because the formatter wants it that way; the Uzbek working week starts on Monday. Month and weekday names are LOWER CASE. FIFTH, the numeric format is DD.MM.YYYY with dots and leading zeros. Time is 24-hour with a colon (14:30). The decimal separator is a comma and the thousands separator a space; the currency name follows the number (1 234,56 soʻm) and is normally spelled out rather than abbreviated. Uzbek has NO grammatical gender and has lost vowel harmony, so any suffix a formatter appends has exactly one form.
